Executive summary

People should not have to visit a gallery to find local art. The Wall brings the art to the places they already are, and makes every piece available to buy with one scan.

The model has been validated in market through a public exhibition in Amman and a signed commercial agreement with a hotel partner. Partner details are available on request. Each installation creates value for three parties at once: the venue shows that it supports local culture, the artist gains an audience and a real chance to sell, and the visitor discovers art without seeking it out.

The numbers. The base case reaches $3.5M revenue and a 21% EBITDA margin by 2031, with EBITDA positive from 2030. A lean first year keeps the peak funding need to $399K; we recommend raising $520K.† Across Jordan, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, the addressable market is about $475M a year, of which $121M is serviceable.

Who pays, and who decides. Space owners, individual buyers and sponsors pay The Wall. Interior designers and architects, who shape new hotels, offices and hospitals, do not pay; they decide where the owner's art budget goes, so The Wall works with them as a channel.

Why Jordan first. Jordan's serviceable market is small, at about $4.6M a year, but it is the lowest-cost place to refine the playbook. The UAE and Saudi Arabia pay 2.2 to 2.5 times more per venue and carry the growth.

Market context

Demand drivers line up in all three markets: rising visitor traffic in Jordan, and a Gulf where corporate and government art spending is growing while the global art market contracts.

908hotel establishments in Jordan with 38,568 rooms, end of 2025MoTA via Jordan News [1]
6.5Minternational visitors to Jordan, Jan–Nov 2025, up 14.6%; tourism revenue $7.16BJordan News [2]
71private hospitals among Jordan's 121 hospitals (2023)Jordan Times [3]
230Kforeign patients treated in Jordan in 2025; medical tourism revenue near $1BPHA via ICE [4]
$21.6BSaudi cultural investment since 2016, as dealers turn to Gulf buyersAl-Monitor / AFP [6]
−12%fall in global art sales in 2024, to $57.5B; UAE corporate collecting has grown since 2020, led by governmentAGBI [5]

Competitive position. No one in Jordan runs rotating, shoppable art programs across commercial venues at scale; the alternatives are ad-hoc art buying by hotels, interior designers sourcing pieces project by project, and a small number of galleries. In the Gulf, art consultancies already serve corporates, so The Wall competes there on rotation, local-artist storytelling and in-venue sales data rather than on collection building alone.

Market size

About $475M a year is addressable, $121M is serviceable, and the 2031 plan captures $3.5M, or 2.9% of the serviceable market.

Sizing is bottom-up: target venues per segment, multiplied by the annual revenue each venue can generate (program fee plus sales commission). It is not a share of the global art market. UAE and Saudi values apply 2.5× and 2.2× the Jordan price.

Business model

The Wall works on consignment, so it carries no inventory risk. Venue fees cover the fixed cost of curation and installation; sales commission grows with the network.

Why designers and architects take part

They will not add a new business line, and The Wall does not ask them to. The proposition works where art is already in their scope:

  • Hotels, large offices and hospitals. Art is a standard line in the furniture, fixtures and equipment (FF&E) or fit-out package. Designers already have to source it, often through consultants or overseas catalogues and under deadline. The Wall delivers a curated, sized and priced selection in 5 working days, then supplies and installs it.
  • A better project. Local art helps meet hotel brand standards for a sense of place, photographs well, and gives the firm a story to publish.
  • No cost and no risk. The owner or contractor contracts with and pays The Wall; the designer recommends and approves.
  • Full disclosure. Many firms cannot accept supplier commissions. Each firm chooses either a disclosed 10% referral fee or a 10% discount passed to its client.

Where art is outside their scope, as in small office fit-outs and most residential work, The Wall goes directly to the owner. Designers and architects are measured on projects referred and won, not on revenue.

Go-to-market

Every approach starts with the live hotel installation and a low-risk first step: a 90-day pilot at 50% of list for space owners, and a free art concept for one live project for specifiers.

Space owners

  1. Lead with the case study: the hotel installation, with photography, a partner testimonial and early engagement and sales data.
  2. Use warm introductions: the founder's network, investor circles, the Jordan Hotels Association, the Private Hospitals Association and chambers of commerce.
  3. Invite prospects to the wall: a short visit, a phone scan and a sample engagement report.
  4. Pilot against three agreed KPIs: scans, sales, and guest or staff feedback, reported monthly.
  5. Convert at day 75 to an annual program, and propose a second zone or property in the same group.

Specifiers: The Wall Trade

The Wall Trade makes The Wall the easiest art supplier for a designer to recommend and for a contractor to buy from. Designers and architects pay nothing.

  • Referral or discount: a disclosed 10% referral fee, or the same 10% passed to the client; the firm chooses. Contractors receive trade pricing on supply-and-install packages.
  • Specification-ready catalogue: dimensions, price, lead time and high-resolution images for renders and mood boards.
  • Free concept for a live project: a curated selection for one space within 5 working days.
  • Commission service: site-specific work from a vetted artist, with fixed milestones.
  • Turnkey supply and installation: framing, delivery, installation, insurance and handover documents.

Recruitment

  1. Founding roster: every artist from the validation pilots is invited as a Founding Artist, with a guaranteed first placement.
  2. Open calls twice a year, with a published brief, a jury and clear selection criteria.
  3. Art schools: graduate shows at Jordanian art and design faculties, and an annual Graduate Wall.
  4. Associations and collectives: referral partnerships and joint open calls.
  5. Galleries as partners: a referral share for represented artists who also want commercial placements.
  6. Peer nominations: each roster artist nominates two peers a year.
  7. Digital scouting of Jordanian, Arab and diaspora artists on Instagram and Behance.

The roster target is 60 artists in year one and 250 by year three, kept selective to protect the curation. Each roster artist is guaranteed at least two placements a year. In return, artists provide original work only, a 90-day consignment per rotation, one retail price across all channels, and rights for The Wall to photograph and promote the work.

      Lean-launch assumption. This assumption cuts the cost of office, manpower and the app in the first year. In 2027 The Wall runs with two people (the founder plus one curator and operations lead), with no office rent or overheads, and a lean first app build of $45K instead of $90K. Installation and transport are handled by freelancers paid per rotation, already included in direct costs. Office costs start in 2028, when the team grows to 11 people with the UAE launch. Without these cuts, the raise would be about $750K.

      SWOT

      The Wall's advantage is a validated model that no one in Jordan runs today, built on a low cost base. Its exposure is a small home market and a sales rate not yet measured at scale.

      Strengths Internal

      • Validated in market: a public exhibition and a signed hotel agreement
      • First mover in Jordan for rotating, shoppable venue art
      • Consignment model with no inventory risk
      • Value for venue, artist and buyer at once
      • Recurring fees plus sales upside
      • QR data proves engagement, which galleries and designers cannot

      Weaknesses Internal

      • Sell-through per venue not yet measured at scale
      • Every rotation is a physical installation
      • Depends on a small curation team
      • Brand not yet known to Gulf buyers
      • Cash-negative until 2030

      Opportunities External

      • Corporate and government art spending growing in the Gulf
      • New hotels and giga-projects in Saudi Arabia need local identity
      • Medical tourism makes private hospitals image-conscious
      • Designers, architects and contractors specifying art into new projects
      • Cultural sponsorship by banks and telcos; prints and office art leasing

      Threats External

      • Gulf consultancies and galleries copy the rotation model
      • Hospitality budgets cut in a regional downturn
      • Damage or theft of works in public spaces
      • Venues buy directly from artists
      • Payment, VAT and art shipping rules differ by country

      Designed in from day one: a 12-month non-circumvention clause, backed by value venues cannot get alone (rotation, insurance, data); and insurance, mounting standards and venue liability terms against damage.
